en: Their spears bore mail pennons,
And their arts of war
Each appeared distinct.
Their horses’ necks arched like swans,
They rode beasts of many kinds,
Finding no enemy to fight,
They rode about pouring out their wrath.
A thought occurred
To your formidable elder Joltoy:
“There is a ditch left by our fathers,
There is light within darkness,
There is a refuge if one flees in fright,
And there is a saying: before an angry man,
Oh, my child, do not make a show of force.
If you seek livestock, go early,
Once twilight falls, the eye cannot see,
Head off coming strife before it arrives,
Once a quarrel starts, words cannot reach it.
I shall bring them to reason,
Fold my hands, offer them food,
And bow my head, saying, ‘Stay,’
If they heed me and submit to reason,
Let me strike with honeyed words,
If he bristles and refuses to talk,
I shall seize him by the collar.
I shall forestall the quarrel,
I shall block the violent man’s path.
Wisdom’s husbandman, Akjoltoy,
With the majesty of a vast host,
Whose every utterance was sweet,
A fluent, free-speaking servant,
A servant well prepared in speech,
In great and restless haste,
His surpassing resourcefulness revealed,
Kulunsur, huge as a bare mountain,
Sprang and ran like an arrow,
And loaded his gold upon a camel.
Kulunsur and the red camel,
To those two raging men,
To the giants Ebegey and Kögöy,
He led them forth as gifts.
Warriors, you have come
From your homeland,
You have set out from your people;
Here is the khan, and here am I,
If you advance, here lies Talas,
Here am I, the eloquent Akjoltoy!
If you truly are khans,
You will pass for lions;
If you are witless, worthless men,
If you are fools who understand no words,
You will cut off the offered head.
The red camel is the gift, and I am the sacrifice—
So your Akjoltoy spoke eloquently.
Ebegey and Kögöy, two giants,
If you two will come to your senses,
You are the ones to whom I speak,
You are my shining dark eyes.
You have stood for deeds of renown,
We are kinsmen of a single root;
If you will not heed reason or words,
You are wretches who ruin the cause.
No Chinese foe with a red-tasseled spear
Is here, shouting and thrusting;
No fearsome enemy is here
Who comes raging against us,
With a feud from ages past.
Consider where this deed will lead;
I bow my neck before what is right,
I offer all my worldly wealth.
Our roots are one, so let us unite;
Our pastures adjoin, so let us stand together.
Our faith is shared, our lives are one—
I say that we must unite.
Though we wage slaughter for forty years,
Though we raid horses with battle cries,
We are steeds that never tire.
Though slaughter lasts for forty years,
Though we clash in combat,
Though we don blood-soaked caps,
Destroying property and taking peace away,
Piercing lungs and taking heads,
Though we become bitter enemies,
We are kin who cannot endure separation.
Ebegey and Kögöy, two lions,
If you are heroes, you will understand:
No one can break the strength
Of a small people firmly united,
But everyone commands the sons
Of a numerous people without unity.
If we stand firm by our pledged word,
If we face the foe that faces us,
Can any cold-hearted invader come
Boasting and playing the hero,
And defeat us in battle?!
If divided, shall we not be overcome,
And the heroes’ backs be broken?
Will not the many enemies who hate us
Overrun and slaughter us,
Quenching the fire we have kindled,
Plundering and laying waste,
Until our battling foe is satisfied
And the heroes’ fortune is broken!
If heads are cut off, the people will be thrown into turmoil,
And the triumphant enemy will rejoice.
Ebegey and Kögöy, two lions,
Accept the livestock offered to you.
As for the weighty words just spoken,
Whether profound or shallow,
Look deeply into their meaning!—
So Akjoltoy spoke,
Folding his hands and presenting the gift,
Sharpening his precious tongue;
Your elder, the venerable Akjoltoy,
Spoke on unwaveringly.
When they witnessed this deed,
Ebegey and Kögöy, the two lions,
Lowered their banners to the ground,
And from their twin thoroughbred steeds
Leapt down and ran forward.
Speaking softly and gravely,
And began to address Akjoltoy:
“Akjoltoy, who came between us,
Wisdom’s husbandman, equal to a vast host,
Are you our elder Akjoltoy?
You are our guiding saint who lends us aid,
Our deeply rooted, immovable plane tree,
A thoroughbred who would not weary
Though journeying for six months,
A kinsman who would never abandon us
Whenever hardship came.
Your words are sweet as sugar,
And your gaze is like a lion’s.
Wise master of understanding,
Akjoltoy sees from afar
The calamities of both kin and foe.
Seeking the broad land of Talas,
Seeking the noble hero Kenen,
We came to pitch our camp,
To raise the war cry against
The Chinese khagan in the uplands,
And become true allies.
We exhausted all our horses,
Consumed all our provisions,
And traveled onward in desperate haste,
Galling every mount,
Weighing heavily upon every heart,
Wearing out our colts until they aged,
Exhausting every horse,
Crossing passes and treading over stones,
And pressing mightily onward.
The forty tribes stirred like stars,
Becoming friends until Judgment Day;
We made firm our word of unity
And swore never to part,
And journeyed here of our own will
To settle upon his pastures.
Our wish to become Kenen’s companions
Had long been spoken;
Our two eyes had become four with watching.
We intended to stir battle against the foe,
To keep the heirs of the treasured people
From humiliation by the cruel,
And willingly receive and protect them—
That alone was our purpose.
If we camped beside Kenen,
Smashed the vaunting enemy
And spilled his blood,
And if hardship came to Kangkay,
Stood beside him as support—
That alone was my desire!”
What else could their elder Akjoltoy do?
After the heroes had spoken thus,
Ebegey and Kögöy, the two lions,
Having accepted his skillful counsel,
Resolved wisely and made a covenant,
Binding their promise firmly.
They slaughtered a mare,
And, to become unquestioned kinsmen,
Dipped their hands in its blood.
Reaching agreement in grave words,
Splitting even a black hair exactly in two,
Winning riches wherever they fought,
They became trusted kinsmen.
While matters stood thus,
With a swift and splendid horse
And a letter small as a palm,
Brandishing a tasselled spear,
Zhelzhetpes equipped a messenger
And sent him to hero Kenen,
Entrusting him with the news.
“All that was needed has been set underway;
Baabedin Kenen, baabedin!
Your warriors have joined the host;
Ebegey and Kögöy, the two lions,
Have become your companions!
Led here by God and destined to share your salt,
To settle in the upper reaches of Talas
And become your companions,
The heroes Ebegey and Kögöy have come;
The greatest fortune, prosperity, and happiness
Have come to be yours!”
So the messenger spoke,
Delivering the news.
When he heard these tidings,
The formidable dark-maned lion, the precious warrior,
The precious hero and protector of the people,
Prepared hereditary gifts
For the lions Ebegey and Kögöy,
And went to behold the heroes’ faces.
He chose warriors from among the finest,
Prepared horses from among the finest steeds,
Prepared richly ornamented robes,
And made everything complete and even,
Amassing abundant wealth.
He had the sealed mouth opened
Of the treasury inherited from his fathers,
And its countless worldly riches
Scattered without counting them worth a hair.
There were great herds of all four kinds,
And strong double-humped camels;
When Ebegey and Kögöy arrived,
Every manner of delight was there.
In the hollow of Jylgynduu,
Along the storied Talas River,
Now behold a wondrous sight:
The feast for Ebegey and Kögöy.
The horses’ tails were knotted for competition,
And the splendid games and festivities
Were proclaimed to all the people.
The heroes competed for the goat,
In games that proved a man,
Their splendor surpassing all the people.
Their weight and worth were known among thousands,
Their fierce heroic nature was revealed.
They maintained a royal court and became great lords;
Ebegey and Kögöy, the two lions,
Became khans seated upon golden thrones.
The matchless hero Kenen,
And Akjoltoy, husbandman of wisdom,
Became men of sacred grace.
His support reaching multitudes of people,
They called Kenen the lion of lions,
Saying his valor, fortune, and prosperity
Showed him to be the true lion’s offspring,
A hero who had indeed been found.
The valiant hero Kenen arose,
His fortunes full and equal,
With an iron core and copper arms,
A steadfast dark-maned lion,
A hero and protector of the people.
Ebegey, Kögöy, and Akjoltoy
Acted as those who came between,
And they settled there in peace.
They had stirred the stars in the heavens:
My forefather, the lion Manas,
